Logos. A Greek word meaning both word and reason. Logos is a foundational concept spanning pre-Socratic philosophy and Christian theology. In Heraclitus, it denotes the rational, cosmic principle governing all change and unity amid apparent flux. In Christian theology, it names the divine Word—Jesus understood as the principle of creation and redemption made incarnate in human form.

In the pre-Socratic philosopher Heraclitus, logos is the underlying rational order or law that governs all natural processes. Fire symbolizes the constant flux of becoming, but logos explains the hidden harmony and pattern within that flux. Heraclitus emphasized logos as rationality itself—the universal reason accessible through philosophical inquiry. It is not merely personal reason but cosmic intelligence, universal reason permeating all things. The concept influenced Stoic philosophy, which adopted logos as the divine rational principle animating the universe, called pneuma. Every soul, they believed, partakes in this universal logos.

In Christian theology, especially in the Gospel of John, we find these words: "In the beginning was the Logos, and the Logos was with God, and the Logos was God." The theological logos represents divine reason, creative power, and incarnate redemption. Jesus is understood as the logos made flesh, bridging the divine and human realms. Later Christian theology integrated Heraclitean and Platonic philosophy with theology. Logos became a way to articulate how the transcendent God relates to creation and humanity.

There is a beautiful ambiguity in the Greek word logos: it means both word—speech, language—and reason, logic, rationality. This ambiguity enriches both philosophical and theological usage. The concept bridges philosophy and theology: it allows Christian thinkers to claim their faith is rational, grounded in logos, while transcending mere reason. Neoplatonism also inherited and transformed logos, connecting it to the One and the Nous, the divine intellect—a synthesis of Greek philosophical and religious thought.
